newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Banks to join snowballing strikes in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Banks to join snowballing strikes in South Korea.

text.p: Snowballing industrial action threatened South Korean banks on Saturday, but transport chaos was averted when non-union drivers kept trains running on the Seoul subway.
Banking unions announced a one-day stoppage next Saturday, joining a wave of strikes called in to protest at a new labour law that allows worker layoffs.
A decision would be taken on whether to extend the action that could cripple the financial industry, already in trouble because of an economic downturn.
Nurses and orderlies at three more hospitals walked out, bringing to 17 the number of medical centres forced to close all but emergency care.
Meanwhile, the government said stoppages that have idled large swathes of industry, including cars and ships, will cost the country more than $1 billion in lost production by the end of the year.
This was on top of $3.2 billion already lost through stoppages earlier in the year.
Unions claimed 375,000 workers at around 700 worksites had joined the walkout by Saturday. Two union umbrella bodies that represent organised labour claim a combined membership of 1.7 million.

Tellers and clerks at commercial banks and mutual savings firms feel vulnerable because financial market opening is expected to spark a wave of mergers in the heavily protected industry, resulting in job cuts.
Next Saturday's strikes will affect the central Bank of Korea and commercial banks and mutual savings firms in Seoul and the provinces.
Starting immediately, tellers and other unionised staff will refuse to wear uniforms.
Bank unions under the officially recognised Federation of Korean Trade Unions claim to represent 132,000 staff.
Underground trains in Seoul ran on time despite a strike by 9,000 drivers and ticketing staff.
The only inconvenience for an estimated four million passengers who use the system daily was closed ticket booths that forced them to use automated machines.
The subway strike marked a new stage in the industrial action because of its impact on everyday life.
Police were posted at stations to prevent union members from disrupting the service.

"I only waited one minute," said Kim Yoon-hwe, 24, on his way to work. Most Koreans still work a half-day on Saturday. "I haven't felt inconvenienced by the strikes. But I'm sure I will if they go on."
Strikes began on Thursday after the government pushed through the labour law in a clandestine dawn session of the National Assembly along with 10 other bills.

Lee Hong-koo, chairman of the ruling New Korea Party, called a news conference to try to resolve the "misunderstanding" Koreans have about the labour legislation, which also allows companies to introduce flexible working hours and replace strikers.
"We revised the law to protect workers' rights and give management the flexibility it needs to maintain competitiveness," Lee said.
"The goal and reason behind the new law seem to be misunderstood by the people."
Meanwhile, opposition members of the National Assembly ended their sit-down protest in parliament that began immediately after the ruling New Korea Party railroaded through the controversial bills.
"By ramming laws through parliament, Kim has destroyed parliament and thus democracy as well," the National Congress for New Politics and United Liberal Democrats said in a joint statement.
